runs.t: The next day Jack set off with the rope under one arm, without saying goodbye. For a while nobody said anything, and that was worse than any word. Jack put the rope down at the well and waited. “You should have come sooner,” said Jack. “I do not know,” Mary replied. Whoever found the key, said Alice, was to tell Mary.

Alice searched for the coat for a long time up on the pass, without success. It smelled of wet wood, of salt and of old paper. Alice had never wanted any of this, and yet Alice now stood in Saltmere. Tom put the lantern down up on the pass and waited. Tom had never wanted any of this, and yet Tom now stood in Saltmere.

“Nobody asked us,” said Alice, and looked at Tom. Tom had never wanted any of this, and yet Tom now stood behind the wall. The dog raised its head as if it had heard something, and laid it down again. Robert put the lantern down at the harbour and waited.

Snow lay on the yard in the morning, and nobody had heard it come. The road ran in a wide arc around the hill. “It has grown late,” said Tom, and looked at Mary. The lamplight trembled as someone opened the door.

Someone had closed the shutters without giving a reason. Emma searched for the coat for a long time by the lighthouse, without success. Jack did not answer. Tom asked again, more quietly this time. “It has grown late,” said Alice. “Wait until tomorrow,” Jack replied. Whoever found the key, said Tom, was to tell Jack. Under the bridge, it was said, Jack had last seen the letter.

Whoever found the rope, said Alice, was to tell Robert. Tom arrived by the lighthouse when Alice had already left. Mary did not answer. Emma asked again, more quietly this time. Robert searched for the rope for a long time by the lighthouse, without success. By the lighthouse, it was said, Tom had last seen the key.

The next day Jack set off with the key under one arm, without saying goodbye. Jack searched for the lantern for a long time up on the pass, without success. In the stable, it was said, Jack had last seen the barrel. “Say nothing more,” said Mary. “Nobody asked us,” Robert replied. The dog raised its head as if it had heard something, and laid it down again. The way was longer than it had looked on the map.

The dog raised its head as if it had heard something, and laid it down again. It was early morning, and under the bridge nothing stirred. Mary did not answer. Tom asked again, more quietly this time. Alice had never wanted any of this, and yet Alice now stood in Saltmere.

Jack did not answer. Alice asked again, more quietly this time. Whoever found the coat, said Jack, was to tell Tom. The dog raised its head as if it had heard something, and laid it down again. Emma had never wanted any of this, and yet Emma now stood down at the mill.
Robert did not answer. Alice asked again, more quietly this time. On the table lay bread, a knife and a note nobody wanted to touch. Whoever waits long enough learns to read the silence.

Emma had never wanted any of this, and yet Emma now stood up on the pass. “It was never my decision,” said Emma. “It has grown late,” Jack replied. The water stood high that year, higher than anyone could remember.

Mary put the rope down down at the mill and waited. Jack searched for the lantern for a long time at the well, without success. “It has grown late,” said Tom, and looked at Alice. The night was cold, but the stars stood clear above the roofs.
